There early Buddha figures arose with flowing robes and wavy hair. The ruler **Kanishka** of the Kushan Empire promoted Buddhism in the 2nd century. His empire controlled important sections of the Silk Road.

According to legend, Emperor Ming dreamed of a golden figure and had scriptures fetched from the West. They came on a white horse to **Luoyang**. That is why the first Buddhist temple in China is called the **White Horse Temple**. From about 148, the monk **An Shigao** from the Parthian Empire translated texts on meditation. Around 400, **Kumarajiva** from Kucha worked in Chang’an with a large team, and his translations are still read today.

The Chinese monk **Xuanzang** travelled to India from 629 to 645 and brought back hundreds of scriptures. His journey inspired the novel **Journey to the West** with the Monkey King Sun Wukong. In the **Mogao Caves** near Dunhuang, a cave full of scriptures was discovered around 1900. Among them was the **Diamond Sutra** of 868, the oldest dated printed book in the world.

In the **Bamiyan Valley** in Afghanistan stood two huge Buddha statues from the 6th century. They were carved directly into a rock face. The valley lay on a trade route between India and Central Asia. In 2001 the Taliban blew up the statues. Their empty niches in the rock face recall it to this day.

gewusst: The oldest dated printed book in the world is a Buddhist text from the year 868.
The name “Silk Road” is much younger than the trade routes themselves; it dates from the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: The secularisation thesis is an assumption from the sociology of religion. It says that religion loses importance in modern societies. Whether that is true has been lively debated by researchers for decades.
wichtigste: The classic thesis links modernisation with a loss of importance for religion.
Peter L. Berger put forward the thesis in 1967 and later largely withdrew it.
Grace Davie spoke of “believing without belonging”.
José Casanova distinguished three meanings of secularisation.
After 2001 Jürgen Habermas coined the term post-secular society.
In 2007 Charles Taylor described how unbelief became a matter-of-course option.

abschnitte.text: The classic **secularisation thesis** assumes that **modernisation** weakens religion. By this are meant industrialisation, science and an ever more varied society. The sociologist **Max Weber** already spoke of the “disenchantment of the world”. The thesis shaped the sociology of religion into the 1970s. The sociologist **Peter L. Berger** put it forward in 1967 in “The Sacred Canopy”.

In 1999, by contrast, Berger spoke of a “**desecularisation** of the world”. In many parts of the world, he said, religion was still very much alive. He declared Europe to be the exception. In 1994 the sociologist of religion **José Casanova** distinguished three meanings: **differentiation**, **decline** and **privatisation**. Only differentiation, he said, was well supported by evidence, that is, that state, science and religion become separate spheres.

**Thomas Luckmann** argued in “The Invisible Religion” that religion does not disappear. It shifts, he said, from the churches into **private searching for meaning**. The British researcher **Grace Davie** found that many people do believe in something but do not actively belong to a church. Her formula “**believing without belonging**” became a catchphrase.

**Pippa Norris** and **Ronald Inglehart** show in “Sacred and Secular” that religiosity falls where people are economically and socially **secure**. **Rodney Stark**, by contrast, explained religious vitality with **rational choice theory**. Many competing offerings, as in the USA, led to high participation. State churches with a monopoly produced rather more passivity.

In 2001, in his Peace Prize speech “Faith and Knowledge”, the philosopher **Jürgen Habermas** spoke of a **post-secular society**. Secular societies, he said, would have to adjust to the fact that religion continues to exist. In 2007 the Canadian philosopher **Charles Taylor** asked in “A Secular Age” why around 1500 unbelief was almost impossible but today is easy. For him, secular means above all that faith is one option among many. In Switzerland the share of people with no religious affiliation has risen sharply since the 1970s.

gewusst: The sociologist Peter L. Berger first put forward the secularisation thesis himself and later contradicted it.
Max Weber described the modern world as “disenchanted”.

teile.einleitung: The Native American Church is a religious community of Indigenous people in North America. It combines old Indigenous customs with Christian elements. In its services the peyote cactus plays a special role.
wichtigste: The church was officially registered in 1918 in the US state of Oklahoma.
In the church the peyote cactus is regarded as a sacred medicine and sacrament.
Peyote contains the substance mescaline, which strongly changes perception.
The night-time ceremony is led by a Roadman.
In the classic rite the earth altar has the shape of a half-moon.
The Comanche leader Quanah Parker promoted the peyote religion.
Since 1994 a US law has protected religious use of peyote nationwide.

abschnitte.text: At the centre of the services is **peyote**, a small cactus. It is eaten or drunk as a tea. The members see it as a **sacred medicine** and a **sacrament**, that is, a holy sign. Peyote contains the substance **mescaline**. This strongly changes perception. Outside protected religious use, mescaline is banned in many countries, including **Switzerland**.

In the late 19th century the peyote rite spread among many tribes. An important supporter was **Quanah Parker**, the last great leader of the **Comanche**. In 1918 the Native American Church was officially registered in the state of **Oklahoma**. Registering as a church was meant to protect the religious use of peyote from bans. Many founders belonged to tribes that had been resettled in what was then Indian Territory.

The ceremony usually lasts **a whole night** and often takes place in a **tipi**. It is led by the **Roadman**. He guides the participants through the night along the “Peyote Road”. Helpers include the **fire keeper** and the **drummer**. In the so-called **Half-Moon rite** an earth altar is built in the shape of a **half-moon**. A large peyote lies on it, and in front of it a fire burns all night. People pray, sing and drum.

The use of peyote repeatedly led to **disputes in court**. In 1990 the US Supreme Court ruled in the case “Employment Division v. Smith” that a general ban on drugs may also apply to religious use. After that, protection was uncertain. In 1994 Congress therefore amended the **American Indian Religious Freedom Act**. Since then the religious use of peyote by Native Americans has been protected throughout the USA.

gewusst: A saying is attributed to Quanah Parker: the white man goes into his church and talks about Jesus, the Indian goes into his tipi and talks with Jesus.
The Native American Church is regarded as one of the largest religious communities of Indigenous people in North America.

teile.einleitung: Candlemas is a Christian festival on 2 February. In Catholic churches the candles for the whole year are blessed on this day. The festival falls 40 days after Christmas.
wichtigste: Candlemas is celebrated on 2 February.
At Candlemas, candles are blessed in Catholic churches.
The festival falls 40 days after Christmas.
It recalls that Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the Temple.
In the past, Candlemas was an important day in the farming year.

abschnitte.text: On **2 February**, **candles are blessed** in Catholic churches. That is where the name **Candlemas** comes from: in the past the candles for the Mass were consecrated on this day. Many people also bring their own candles. They light them at home, for example during a thunderstorm or in hard times. Often there is a solemn **procession of lights**.

In the church the festival is also called the **Presentation of the Lord**. It falls **40 days after Christmas**. According to the Bible, **Mary and Joseph** brought the infant Jesus to the **Temple** in Jerusalem. There the old **Simeon** recognised in him the saviour and called him a light for all peoples. That is why candles play a large part on this day.

abschnitte.titel: A day in the farming year
abschnitte.text: In the past, Candlemas was an important day in the country. The days grow noticeably longer, and less light was needed in the evening. For maids and farmhands the **year of service** often ended, and some changed farms. There are many **farmers’ sayings** about Candlemas. One says: if it is bright and clear at Candlemas, a long winter is still to come.

gewusst: On the day after Candlemas, 3 February, many Catholic churches give the blessing of St Blaise against sore throats.
In North America people watch a groundhog on 2 February to predict the spring.

teile.einleitung: Raksha Bandhan is a Hindu festival for brothers and sisters. The sister ties a colourful protective band around her brother’s wrist, and the brother promises to be there for her.
wichtigste: Raksha Bandhan is a festival of brothers and sisters.
The sister ties a protective band around her brother’s wrist.
The band is called a rakhi.
It stands for protection and closeness.
The brother often gives his sister a present.
The festival is celebrated at the full moon in the month of Shravana, usually in August.

abschnitte.text: The name **Raksha Bandhan** means roughly “band of protection”. On the festival day the sister ties a colourful band around her brother’s wrist. This band is called a **rakhi**. It can be quite simple or decorated with beads and glitter. The band stands for **protection** and **closeness** between brothers and sisters.

Often the sister first puts a small dot on her brother’s forehead and prays for him. Then she ties the rakhi and gives him something sweet. The brother promises to protect his sister and gives her a **present**. Afterwards the whole family celebrates together.

Raksha Bandhan is celebrated on the **full moon** in the Hindu month of **Shravana**. In our calendar that is usually in **August**. The festival is especially popular in northern India and in Nepal. Today friends sometimes tie a rakhi on each other too, as a sign of friendship.

gewusst: Before the festival, the markets in India sell thousands of different rakhis in all colours.
Anyone who lives far away often has their rakhi sent by post by their sister.

teile.einleitung: The Mahmood Mosque in Zurich was opened in 1963. It is regarded as the first mosque in Switzerland built specifically as a mosque, and it has a small minaret.
wichtigste: The Mahmood Mosque stands in Zurich on Forchstrasse.
It was opened in 1963.
It is regarded as the first mosque in Switzerland.
Its minaret is about 18 metres high.
It belongs to the Muslim Ahmadiyya community.

abschnitte.text: The **Mahmood Mosque** stands in Zurich on **Forchstrasse**. It was opened in **1963** and was the first mosque to be built in Switzerland. The building is rather small and plain. Striking is the white **minaret**, about 18 metres high. A minaret is the tower of a mosque.

The mosque belongs to the **Ahmadiyya**, a Muslim community that arose in India in the 19th century. It is there for prayers, festivals and meetings of the community. Often the community also invites visitors who would like to get to know Islam.

Today there are many Muslim prayer rooms in Switzerland. Most, however, are in ordinary buildings, for example in converted flats or warehouses. Mosques with a minaret are rare. Since a popular vote in 2009, the **Federal Constitution** has forbidden the building of new minarets. Existing minarets such as the one in Zurich were allowed to stay.

gewusst: The minaret of the Mahmood Mosque is one of the few minarets in the whole of Switzerland.
The mosque is named after a leader of the Ahmadiyya community.

teile.einleitung: Odin was the supreme god in Norse mythology. The Vikings and other Norse peoples saw him as the father of the gods. He was regarded as clever, wise and the god of poetry and war.
wichtigste: Odin was the father of the Norse gods.
Among the southern Germanic peoples he was called Wodan or Wotan.
On his shoulders sit the ravens Huginn and Muninn.
According to belief, fallen warriors went to his hall Valhalla.
His weapon is the spear Gungnir.
According to legend, he discovered the runes.

abschnitte.text: **Odin** was at the head of the Norse gods. He ruled in **Asgard**, the world of the gods. He was regarded as especially **clever and wise**. For his wisdom he is said even to have sacrificed an eye, which is why he is often shown **one-eyed**. Among the southern Germanic peoples the father of the gods was called **Wodan** or **Wotan**. Many stories about him are in the **Edda**, old texts from Iceland.

On Odin’s shoulders sit two **ravens**. They are called **Huginn** and **Muninn**, which mean roughly “thought” and “memory”. Every day they fly through the world and tell him what they have seen. Odin’s weapon is the spear **Gungnir**, which is said never to miss its target. He rides **Sleipnir**, a horse with eight legs.

According to the belief of the Norsemen, the **Valkyries** brought brave fallen warriors to Odin. They came to his great hall **Valhalla**. There they feasted, ate and drank. They were to help Odin in the last great battle at the end of the world. In the legend this end of the world is called **Ragnarök**.

The **runes** were the old script of the Germanic peoples. According to the legend, Odin hung for **nine days** from a tree, the world tree **Yggdrasil**. Afterwards he knew the secret of the runes. The story shows how much Odin took upon himself for knowledge. Rune stones with carved signs can still be found today, above all in Scandinavia.

gewusst: Wednesday is named after “Woden’s day”, that is, Odin’s day.
According to the legend, Odin’s horse Sleipnir has eight legs and can run through air and water.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland a Landeskirche, or cantonal church, is a church that a canton has recognised under public law. It is thereby especially connected with the state, but remains independent in questions of faith. Because each canton regulates this itself, there are many differences.
wichtigste: Landeskirchen are recognised by the canton under public law.
Usually the Roman Catholic and the Evangelical Reformed churches are recognised.
In many cantons the Christian Catholic Church is a Landeskirche too.
In most cantons recognised churches may levy church taxes.
In several cantons Jewish communities are also recognised.
In Reformed parishes the members elect their ministers.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **cantons** regulate the relationship between state and religion. A **Landeskirche** is **recognised under public law** by a canton. This means it has special rights and duties, much like a municipality. In its questions of faith, however, it decides for itself. The church is divided into **parishes**.

In most cantons the **Roman Catholic** and the **Evangelical Reformed** churches are recognised. In many cantons the small **Christian Catholic** church is added. It arose in protest against the **infallibility of the pope**, which the First Vatican Council had proclaimed in 1870. Several cantons, including Basel-Stadt, Bern and Zurich, have also recognised **Jewish communities** under public law.

In most cantons the recognised churches may collect **church taxes** from their members. In many cantons **companies** pay church tax too. With the money the churches pay ministers, buildings and social work, for example for families, older people or refugees. Whoever leaves the church no longer pays church tax.

Reformed parishes are organised **democratically**. The members with voting rights elect their **minister** and decide on the budget. The Reformed cantonal churches have a common umbrella organisation. Since **2020** it has been called the **Evangelical Reformed Church of Switzerland**, EKS for short. Before that it was called the Federation of Swiss Protestant Churches.

gewusst: The Christian Catholic Church has its bishop in Bern.
In the cantons of Geneva and Neuchâtel, church and state are more strongly separated than in most other cantons.

teile.einleitung: The Assumption of Mary is a Christian holiday on 15 August. Catholic Christians celebrate that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was taken up into heaven, body and soul, after her life.
wichtigste: The Assumption of Mary is on 15 August.
It celebrates Mary being taken up into heaven.
In the Catholic Church it is a solemnity, the highest rank of feast.
In many Catholic cantons of Switzerland the day is a public holiday.
In many places herbs are blessed on this day.

abschnitte.text: On the **Assumption of Mary**, Catholic Christians remember that Mary was taken up into heaven, **body and soul**, after her life on earth. The Bible says nothing about this. It is an old tradition of the Church. In 1950 Pope **Pius XII** declared it a binding article of faith, a **dogma**. The Orthodox churches celebrate the Feast of the Dormition of Mary on the same day.

In Switzerland each **canton** decides for itself which days are public holidays. In many cantons with a Catholic tradition, 15 August is a day off work, for example in Valais, Ticino or Lucerne. In cantons with a Reformed tradition such as Zurich or Bern, however, it is an ordinary working day. So it can happen that the shops are closed in one canton and open in the neighbouring one.

In many areas, **bunches of herbs** are blessed on the Assumption of Mary. People tie healing herbs and flowers together and take them to church. Afterwards they hang them up at home. In some places there are **processions**, in which a figure of Mary is carried through the streets.

gewusst: The Assumption of Mary falls in the middle of the summer holidays, so many schoolchildren do not even notice that it is a public holiday.
In Italy the day is called “Ferragosto” and is one of the most important holiday days of the summer.

teile.einleitung: Pentecost is one of the great festivals of Christians. They remember that the Holy Spirit came to the disciples of Jesus.
wichtigste: At Pentecost Christians celebrate the coming of the Holy Spirit.
Pentecost is 50 days after Easter.
The word comes from the Greek “pentekoste”, which means “the fiftieth day”.
The story is in the Acts of the Apostles in the Bible.
Pentecost is regarded as the birthday of the Church.
In many cantons Whit Monday is a public holiday.

abschnitte.text: The story is in the **Acts of the Apostles** in the Bible. The disciples of Jesus were gathered in Jerusalem. Suddenly there came a rushing sound like a storm. Above their heads appeared **flames like tongues of fire**. The disciples were filled with the **Holy Spirit** and could speak in many languages.

Pentecost is celebrated **50 days after Easter**. That is where the name comes from: the Greek word **pentekoste** means “the fiftieth day”. Because Easter falls on a different date every year, Pentecost moves too. It is always in May or June.

The Holy Spirit is often shown as a **dove**. **Fire** and **wind** are also signs of it. After Pentecost the disciples began to tell the message of Jesus everywhere. That is why Pentecost is also called the **birthday of the Church**.
In Switzerland Pentecost is a Sunday. **Whit Monday** is a public holiday in many cantons, when schools and many shops are closed. Many families use the long weekend for outings.

gewusst: Judaism also has a festival 50 days after Passover, called Shavuot.
The peony is called “Pfingstrose” in German, Pentecost rose, because it often blooms around Pentecost.

teile.einleitung: A solstice fire is a large fire lit at the solstice. Especially in summer, around the longest day of the year, the custom is widespread in the Alps. With the fire people celebrate the sun and the light.
wichtigste: The summer solstice is around 21 June.
On this day the day is at its longest.
The winter solstice around 21 December is the shortest day.
There are two solstices in the year.
Solstice fires often burn on mountains and hills.
The St John’s fire on 24 June is related to the solstice fire.

abschnitte.text: Around **21 June** is the **summer solstice**. Then the sun stands at its highest at midday where we live, and the day is at its **longest**. After that the days become shorter again. Around **21 December** is the **winter solstice**, when the day is shortest and the night longest. So there are **two** solstices in the year. In between, in spring and autumn, lie the **equinoxes**.

Since ancient times people have honoured the power of the **sun** with fire. The fire stands for **light** and **warmth**. People hoped that it would bring luck and drive away misfortune. In the **Alps** solstice fires are often lit on **mountains and hills**. There they can be seen far down into the valley, and on that night many fires shine at the same time.

An old custom is **jumping over the fire**. In the past, young people jumped over the low fire when it had already burned down. This was meant to bring luck and health. Today this is rarer because of the risk of injury. Often there is singing, eating and celebrating around the fire.

**24 June** is **St John’s Day**, the feast of John the Baptist. The **St John’s fire** on this day is related to the old solstice fire. In this way the Church linked an old custom with a Christian festival. In Switzerland there are also the **mountain-top fires** on 1 August, the national holiday. They have a different occasion, however.

gewusst: In the Southern Hemisphere, for example in Australia, June has the shortest day of the year.
On 21 June in Switzerland it is light for about 16 hours.

teile.einleitung: Santiago de Compostela is a city in the north-west of Spain. It is one of the most important pilgrimage destinations for Christians. The famous Way of St James leads here.
wichtigste: **Santiago de Compostela** lies in Galicia in the north-west of Spain.
The apostle **James** is said to be buried there.
The **Way of St James** ends in Santiago.
The sign of the pilgrims is the **scallop shell**.
Ways of St James also lead through Switzerland.
The old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: James was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus. According to tradition, his tomb was discovered in Galicia in the 9th century. A church arose over the tomb, and later it became the great **cathedral**. Soon pilgrims came from all over Europe. Alongside Rome and Jerusalem, Santiago became one of the most important pilgrimage destinations of the Middle Ages.

The **Way of St James** is not a single path but a network of paths from many countries. Especially well known is the Camino Francés through northern Spain. Pilgrims often walk for weeks. Anyone who walks at least the last 100 kilometres on foot receives a certificate in Santiago, the **Compostela**. Today people make the pilgrimage for religious reasons, but also for the joy of walking or in order to reflect.

The sign of the pilgrims is the **scallop shell**. You see it on rucksacks and as a waymark on many paths. In the cathedral there is a huge incense burner, the **botafumeiro**. At special services it is swung on a rope through the nave.

abschnitte.titel: Ways of St James in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Ways of St James also lead through Switzerland. A well-known route begins at Lake Constance and leads via **Einsiedeln**, Fribourg and Lausanne to **Geneva**. From there the way continues through France to Spain. Many pilgrims spend the night on the way in monasteries or simple hostels. Yellow signposts and shell signs show the way.

gewusst: When St James’s Day, 25 July, falls on a Sunday, Santiago celebrates a Holy Year with especially many pilgrims.
The old town of Santiago de Compostela has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.

teile.einleitung: When people move to a new country, they take their faith with them. That is why migration has greatly changed the religious landscape of Switzerland. This page shows which communities arose through immigration and flight.
wichtigste: Already after 1685, French Protestants, the **Huguenots**, fled to Reformed Swiss cities.
Many Muslims in Switzerland have roots in the Western Balkans or in Turkey.
The largest Hindu community is formed by Tamils from Sri Lanka.
For Tibetan refugees the Tibet Institute was founded in Rikon ZH in 1968.
Orthodox churches and many migrant churches have grown through immigration.
For Catholic newcomers there are missions in other languages.

abschnitte.titel: Refugees for their faith in the past
abschnitte.text: In the year 1685 the French king revoked the **Edict of Nantes**, which had given Protestants protection. After that many **Huguenots** fled to Reformed areas such as Geneva, Bern and Zurich. They brought knowledge and skills with them, for example in watchmaking and the textile trade. Even then it was clear: anyone who has to flee because of their faith seeks a place where they can live it freely.

From the 1960s many **migrant workers** came to Switzerland, at first mainly from Italy, later also from Spain, Portugal, Yugoslavia and Turkey. In the 1990s many people fled the wars in the former Yugoslavia. That is why many Muslims in Switzerland today come from Kosovo, North Macedonia, Bosnia or Turkey. Since the civil war in Sri Lanka from 1983, many **Tamils** have come, who founded Hindu temples.

From the 1960s Switzerland took in refugees from **Tibet**. So that they could continue to practise their religion, the Tibet Institute was founded in **Rikon** in the Töss valley in 1968. It is a Buddhist monastery in which monks live. The Tibetan community in Switzerland is regarded as the largest in Europe.

For Catholics of other languages, **missions in other languages** arose after the Second World War, at first mainly Italian ones. The **Orthodox churches** grew through immigration from Serbia, Romania, Russia and Eritrea. They often hold their services in the language of their country of origin. In addition there are **migrant churches**: Christian communities founded by newcomers themselves, often with an African, Latin American or Asian background.

The Greek word **diaspora** means “scattering”. At first it meant Jews who lived outside the land of Israel. Today the term generally describes communities that practise their religion far from the region they come from. Many communities in the diaspora keep festivals, language and customs alive and at the same time adapt to the new country.

gewusst: Many migrant churches rent rooms for their services from the Reformed or Catholic cantonal churches.
The Huguenots helped Geneva to become a well-known city of watchmaking.

teile.einleitung: A new religious movement is a religious group that arose only recently, mostly in the 19th or 20th century. The study of religion uses this term because it is neutral. Some of these groups are harmless, and some are very controversial.
wichtigste: The term “new religious movement” is value-neutral, while “sect” sounds disparaging in everyday speech.
In 1988 the sociologist Eileen Barker founded the information centre INFORM.
L. Ron Hubbard founded Scientology, based on his 1950 book “Dianetics”.
Sun Myung Moon founded the Unification Church in Seoul in 1954.
In the 1970s, people in German-speaking countries often spoke of “youth religions”.
In 1994, 48 members of the Order of the Solar Temple died in Switzerland.
Some groups became known through serious crimes and tragedies.

abschnitte.text: In everyday speech you often hear the word **“sect”**. But it sounds disparaging and is used inconsistently. The **study of religion** therefore prefers to speak of **new religious movements**. The term describes groups without prejudice. The British sociologist **Eileen Barker** of the London School of Economics founded the information centre **INFORM** in 1988. It is meant to give factual information about such groups.

Among the well-known new religious movements is **Scientology**. Its founder **L. Ron Hubbard** published the book **“Dianetics”** in 1950 and founded the first Church of Scientology in the USA in 1954. The organisation is controversial in several countries. The **Unification Church** was founded in Seoul in 1954 by **Sun Myung Moon**. It became known, among other things, for its mass weddings.

In the **1970s** many young people joined new groups. In German-speaking countries people therefore spoke of **“youth religions”**. The Protestant sect commissioner **Friedrich-Wilhelm Haack** made the term well known. Today it is seen as imprecise, because the members grew older. In Switzerland there are specialist centres that give information and advice about such groups.

Some groups became known through terrible events. In 1978, more than 900 members of Jim Jones’s “Peoples Temple” died in **Jonestown** in Guyana. In **October 1994**, 48 members of the **Order of the Solar Temple** died in **Cheiry FR** and **Salvan VS**, with more in Canada. In 1995 the Japanese group **Aum Shinrikyo** carried out a sarin gas attack on the Tokyo subway. Such cases set off debates about how states should deal with groups that take people over.

gewusst: In Switzerland too there are many small new religious movements, and most of them hardly attract attention.
Many of today’s large religions were also regarded as new movements in their early days.

teile.einleitung: The Eleusinian Mysteries were secret religious ceremonies in ancient Greece. They were celebrated for over a thousand years in Eleusis near Athens. Anyone who took part had to keep silent, which is why much remains a mystery to this day.
wichtigste: The Mysteries were dedicated to the goddesses Demeter and Persephone.
Eleusis lies north-west of Athens.
The initiated had to keep strict silence, and betrayal could be punished by death.
A procession travelled along the Sacred Way from Athens to Eleusis.
The great hall of initiation was called the Telesterion.
The chief priest was called the Hierophant.
The Mysteries ended at the end of the 4th century AD.

abschnitte.text: At the centre were **Demeter**, the goddess of grain, and her daughter **Persephone**, also called Kore. According to the myth, Persephone was abducted by the god of the underworld. Demeter searched for her in despair, and during this time nothing grew on earth any more. In the underworld Persephone had eaten **pomegranate seeds**. That is why she had to stay there for part of every year. This is how the Greeks explained **winter**, when nothing grows.

Anyone who took part in the Mysteries was **initiated**. The initiated had to promise to reveal nothing. Anyone who did so anyway faced the **death penalty**. That is why ancient authors wrote about it only in hints. To this day nobody knows exactly what happened on the holy night. It is thought that sacred objects were shown and scenes from the myth were acted out.

At the **Greater Mysteries** in autumn, a long procession travelled from Athens to Eleusis. The road was called the **Sacred Way** and was about 20 kilometres long. The participants went on foot. Beforehand they had fasted. Afterwards they drank the **kykeon**, a drink of barley, water and pennyroyal. According to the hymn to Demeter, the grieving goddess had also taken this drink.

In the sanctuary stood the **Telesterion**, a large, almost square hall with many columns and rows of seats. The initiated gathered there at night. The chief priest was called the **Hierophant**, which means “the one who shows the holy things”. Traditionally he came from the family of the **Eumolpidae**. He showed the participants the sacred objects.

The Mysteries were celebrated for over **a thousand years**. Many Romans also had themselves initiated. At the end of the 4th century AD, Emperor **Theodosius I** banned the old pagan cults. In the year 396 the **Visigoths** under Alaric laid waste to the sanctuary. Today you can visit the ruins in Eleusis.

gewusst: Men and women, free people and even slaves could take part in the Mysteries, as long as they spoke Greek.
Today the word “mystery” generally means a secret.

teile.einleitung: In some religions there are rules about what you may eat and what you may not. Devout Jews and Muslims do not eat pork. This rule comes from their holy scriptures.
wichtigste: Devout **Jews** and **Muslims** do not eat **pork**.
In both religions the pig is regarded as unclean.
The Jewish dietary rules are called **kashrut**, and permitted foods are **kosher**.
In Islam permitted foods are called **halal**.
Many schools and canteens in Switzerland also offer food without pork.

abschnitte.text: The Jewish dietary laws are called **kashrut**. Permitted foods are called **kosher**. According to the Torah, you may eat land animals that have cloven hooves and chew the cud, such as cattle, sheep or goats. The pig does have cloven hooves, but it does not chew the cud. That is why it is regarded as unclean and is not eaten.

The **Quran** too says that Muslims should not eat pork. Permitted foods are called **halal**, forbidden ones **haram**. Besides pork, these include alcohol, for example. Many Muslims also take care that gummy bears or other sweets do not contain gelatine from pigs.

In other religions there are other rules: many Hindus do not eat beef, and some live entirely as **vegetarians**. In Christianity there are no such fixed prohibitions. In Switzerland many schools, canteens and hospitals therefore offer menus without pork or vegetarian dishes. That way everyone can eat together, whatever rules they follow.

gewusst: Gelatine is often made from pig skin, which is why gummy bears also come in halal or kosher versions.
In Switzerland more pork is eaten than any other kind of meat.

teile.einleitung: Om is a sacred syllable and a sacred sound. It is especially important in Hinduism, but also in Buddhism, Jainism and among the Sikhs. Many prayers begin or end with Om.
wichtigste: Om is a sacred syllable and a sacred sound.
Many Hindus speak or sing Om at the start of a prayer.
Om is sung long, deep and calm.
According to ancient teaching, Om is made up of the three sounds A, U and M.
A sacred word that is repeated often is called a mantra.
The Om symbol is often seen in temples.
Om is also sacred in Buddhism, in Jainism and among the Sikhs.

abschnitte.text: **Om**, often also written **Aum**, is a sacred word for Hindus. It stands for the divine and for the whole universe. Many **prayers** begin with Om, and often it is also spoken at the end. It is sung **long, deep and calm**. The sound hums through the whole body. Many people become calm as they do so.

According to ancient teaching, Om is made up of **three sounds**: **A**, **U** and **M**. Spoken together they sound like “Om”. The three sounds are interpreted in different ways. They often stand for waking, dreaming and deep sleep. The three sounds are followed by a **silence**, which also belongs to the Om.

A sacred word or short saying that is said or sung again and again is called a **mantra**. Om is the best-known mantra. It also stands at the start of many other mantras. A well-known Buddhist mantra is **“Om mani padme hum”**. The repetitions are often counted on a string of prayer beads.

Om has its own **written symbol** in Indian script. It is seen in **temples**, on altars and in pictures. Om is also known all over the world through **yoga**. Many yoga classes, in Switzerland too, begin or end with a shared Om. Om is not only important for Hindus: in **Buddhism**, **Jainism** and among the **Sikhs** it is also regarded as sacred.

gewusst: The Om symbol even exists as a character of its own in the computer character set Unicode.
In Tibet the mantra “Om mani padme hum” is written on many prayer flags and prayer wheels.

teile.einleitung: Every religion has special days on which believers celebrate, pray or fast. In Switzerland some Christian holidays are also days off from work and school. For the holidays of other religions there are often special rules.
wichtigste: Pentecost recalls the sending of the **Holy Spirit**.
Ascension Day always falls on a Thursday.
The **Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer** is on the third Sunday in September.
The Islamic **Festival of Sacrifice** recalls Abraham.
**Yom Kippur** is the Jewish Day of Atonement.
Schoolchildren can be excused from lessons on the high holidays of their religion.

abschnitte.text: **Pentecost** is celebrated 50 days after Easter. According to the Bible, the Holy Spirit came down on the disciples of Jesus. Whit Monday is a day off in most cantons. **Ascension Day** falls on the 40th day of the Easter season, if you count Easter Sunday as the first day. That is why it always lands on a Thursday. **Corpus Christi** is celebrated with processions on the second Thursday after Pentecost and is a day off mainly in Catholic cantons such as Lucerne.

The **Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer** is a holiday for the whole of Switzerland. In most cantons it is celebrated on the third Sunday in September. The day was observed by Catholics and Reformed Christians together and was meant to bring the denominations together. Geneva celebrates the “Jeûne genevois” instead, also in September.

The Islamic **Festival of Sacrifice**, in Arabic “Eid al-Adha”, recalls Abraham, who wanted to obey God. God had an animal sacrificed in place of his son. **Yom Kippur** is the highest Jewish holiday: believers fast for about 25 hours and ask for forgiveness. **Nowruz** means “new day” and is a New Year festival at the beginning of spring, around 21 March. It is celebrated in Iran, by Kurds and by the Baha’i.

In many cantons, parents can apply for an **exemption** for their child on the high holidays of its religion. This means the child is excused from lessons on request. The exact rules are set by the cantons, because schools are a matter for the cantons in Switzerland. That way children of different religions can celebrate their most important festivals with their families.

gewusst: Because Easter falls on a different date every year, Ascension Day, Pentecost and Corpus Christi also move around the calendar.
Islamic festivals shift by about eleven days every year, because the Islamic calendar follows the moon.

teile.einleitung: The cult of Mithras was a secret religion in the Roman Empire. Its followers worshipped the god Mithras, who originally came from Persia, and met in dark, cave-like rooms.
wichtigste: Mithras was originally a Persian god.
The followers met in a room called a Mithraeum.
The most important cult image shows Mithras killing a bull.
Especially many soldiers belonged to the cult.
There were seven grades of initiation, and the highest was called Pater.
According to the myth, Mithras was born from a rock.
In 1993 a Mithraeum was discovered in Martigny in Valais.

abschnitte.text: **Mithras** was originally a god from **Persia**. The Romans took over his name and made it into a **secret cult**. Only the initiated were allowed to take part, and they did not speak about it. That is why much is known today only from excavations and images. According to the myth, Mithras came forth from a **rock**. He is therefore also called the “rock-born”.

The followers met in a **Mithraeum**. This was usually a dark, long room meant to recall a cave. Along the sides stood **benches** on which people reclined for the shared meal. At the front, in the centre, the most important cult image could be seen: Mithras killing a **bull**. This scene is called the **tauroctony**.

In the cult of Mithras, especially many **soldiers** were involved. That is why many Mithraea were found near military camps on the edge of the Roman Empire, for example on the Rhine and the Danube. **Merchants** and officials also belonged to it. According to what we know today, women were not admitted.

Anyone who joined the cult rose through **seven grades of initiation**. The lowest grade was called **Raven**. Each grade was linked to a **planet**. The highest grade was called **Pater**, Latin for father. The Pater led the community of a Mithraeum.

The cult of Mithras existed in what is now Switzerland too. In **Martigny** in Valais, the Roman **Forum Claudii Vallensium**, a Mithraeum was excavated in **1993**. In Roman times Martigny was the main town of Valais. The remains can be visited today. With the rise of Christianity, the cult of Mithras disappeared in the 4th century.

gewusst: Many Mithraea were built underground so that they would be dark like a cave.
Remains of Mithraea have been found beneath several churches in Rome.

teile.einleitung: Medina is a city in Saudi Arabia. After Mecca it is the second holiest city in Islam, because the Prophet Muhammad spent his last years here and his tomb is here.
wichtigste: Medina lies in the west of Saudi Arabia.
After Mecca it is the second holiest city of Islam.
Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina in the year 622.
This move, the Hijra, marks the start of the Islamic calendar.
The tomb of Muhammad lies in the Prophet’s Mosque.

abschnitte.text: Medina used to be called **Yathrib**. In the year **622** the Prophet **Muhammad** moved with his followers from Mecca to Yathrib, because he was under pressure in Mecca. This move is called the **Hijra**. It marks the start of the **Islamic calendar**. After that the city was given the name “Madinat an-Nabi”, the City of the Prophet, or **Medina** for short.

In Medina, Muhammad built one of the first mosques. From it grew the huge **Prophet’s Mosque**. Under a green dome there lies the **tomb of Muhammad**, who died in Medina in the year 632. Over the centuries the mosque was enlarged again and again and is one of the largest mosques in the world.
Many Muslims who travel to Mecca for the great pilgrimage, the **Hajj**, also visit Medina. A visit to Medina is not one of the duties of the pilgrimage, however. It is regarded as especially worthy.

gewusst: The green dome over Muhammad’s tomb is one of the best-known buildings in the Islamic world.
In the Islamic calendar, years are counted from the Hijra in the year 622.

teile.einleitung: Songlines are sung paths of the Aboriginal people, the indigenous inhabitants of Australia. The songs tell how ancestral beings shaped the land in the time of creation. At the same time they help people find their way in the landscape.
wichtigste: Songlines follow the paths of the creator ancestors through the land.
They served as a sung map with waterholes and landmarks.
The Anangu call the time of creation and its laws Tjukurpa.
Bruce Chatwin made songlines known worldwide in 1987.
Since October 2019, climbing Uluru has been banned.

abschnitte.text: In the stories of the **Aboriginal people**, ancestral beings wandered through the land in the time of creation. In doing so they shaped mountains, rivers and waterholes. The **songlines** follow exactly these paths. The verses name landmarks in the order in which you meet them. Anyone who knows the songs can therefore find **waterholes** and routes even over long distances. The songs are thus a **sung map**.

Around 1900 the ethnologists **Baldwin Spencer** and **Francis Gillen** translated the Arrernte word “alcheringa” as “dream times”. From this came the English **Dreaming**, in German **Traumzeit**. Many Aboriginal people find the term imprecise. It is not about dreams but about an order of creation that is always present. The **Anangu** in the centre of Australia call it **Tjukurpa**. It includes creation stories, law and morality.

A famous songline tells of the **Seven Sisters**. They flee across the continent from a pursuer and finally become stars. These stars are the **Pleiades**, a star cluster in the night sky. In 2017 the National Museum of Australia dedicated a large exhibition to the story.

**Uluru** is a mighty red rock in central Australia and sacred to the Anangu. For decades the traditional owners asked visitors not to climb it. Since **26 October 2019** climbing it has been banned entirely. Visitors can, however, walk around the rock on foot.

The British writer **Bruce Chatwin** wrote the book “The Songlines” in 1987. It combines travel writing, narrative and thoughts on the life of nomads. The book became a bestseller and made songlines known worldwide. It was also criticised for inaccuracies.

gewusst: Some songlines are so long that they lead right across the whole of Australia.
The Seven Sisters of the Aboriginal people are the same star cluster that is called the Pleiades in Europe.

teile.einleitung: Ra, also called Re, was the sun god in ancient Egypt. The Egyptians believed that he sails across the sky in a boat every day and so brings the day.
wichtigste: Ra was the Egyptian sun god.
According to belief, he sailed across the sky in a solar barque every day.
He is often shown with a falcon’s head and a sun disc.
At night he travelled through the underworld.
There he fought the giant serpent Apophis.
The pharaohs called themselves “son of Ra”.

abschnitte.text: For the ancient Egyptians the **sun** was vital, because it made plants grow. In it they saw the power of the god **Ra**. He was regarded as one of the most important gods and often as the creator of the world. An important place of his worship was the city of **Heliopolis**, which means “city of the sun”.
Ra is often shown as a man with the head of a **falcon**. Above his head hovers a round **sun disc**. It is often encircled by a snake, the **uraeus**. It was meant to protect the god.

The Egyptians believed that Ra sails across the sky in a **solar barque**. A barque is a boat, and on the Nile the Egyptians themselves mostly travelled by boat. The morning sun was called **Khepri** and was shown as a **scarab**. A scarab is a beetle that rolls a ball in front of it, just as the sun rolls across the sky.

In the evening the sun set. Then, according to belief, Ra travelled through the **underworld**. There the evil giant serpent **Apophis** waited, wanting to stop the solar barque. Ra and his helpers defeated it every night. That is why the sun rose again in the morning.

The kings of Egypt bore the title **“son of Ra”**. In this way they showed that they were linked with the sun god. Later Ra merged with the god **Amun** to become **Amun-Re**, the most important god of the New Kingdom.

gewusst: Many pharaohs’ names contain the name of the sun god, for example Ramesses, which means “Ra has given birth to him”.
The tips of obelisks were often gilded so that they gleamed in the sunlight.

teile.einleitung: Sigmund Freud was an Austrian doctor and the founder of psychoanalysis. He also dealt with the question of why people are religious. His critical writings on religion set off many discussions.
wichtigste: Freud lived from 1856 to 1939, most of the time in Vienna.
He founded psychoanalysis, a teaching about the unconscious.
In 1927 he called religion an illusion in a work.
He traced the idea of God back to the longing for a protecting father.
The Zurich pastor Oskar Pfister contradicted him in 1928.
Freud’s views on religion are disputed to this day.

abschnitte.text: **Sigmund Freud** was born in 1856 and worked as a doctor in **Vienna**. He developed **psychoanalysis**. It assumes that many feelings and wishes are **unconscious** and yet influence our actions. Freud came from a Jewish family but was not a believer himself. In 1938 he had to flee from the Nazis to London, where he died in 1939.

In 1907 Freud wrote the essay “Obsessive Actions and Religious Practices”. He compared religious **rituals** with the actions of people with an **obsessional neurosis**. Such people repeat certain actions always in exactly the same way. Freud therefore called religion a universal obsessional neurosis of humankind. In “**Totem and Taboo**” of 1912/13 he told a conjecture about prehistoric times from which totemism and religion were supposed to have arisen.

In the work “**The Future of an Illusion**” of 1927, Freud interprets religious teachings as **wish fulfilments**. For him an illusion is not necessarily false, but it is carried by a wish. The adult, he said, feels helpless towards the world as the child once did. That is why he imagines God as a powerful, **protecting father**. Freud hoped that science would one day replace religion.

The Zurich pastor **Oskar Pfister** was a psychoanalyst and a friend of Freud. In 1928 he replied with the work “The Illusion of a Future”. He defended faith and held Freud’s hope in science to be an illusion itself. The writer **Romain Rolland** spoke of an “**oceanic feeling**” of connection with the universe. Freud discussed this idea in 1930 in “Civilization and Its Discontents”.

Freud’s critique of religion had great influence on psychology and philosophy. Many experts today consider his assumptions about prehistoric times unproven. Scholars of religion also stress that religion has many different sides. Believers do not see their faith as an illusion. So Freud remains an important but disputed thinker.

gewusst: Despite their dispute about religion, Freud and the devout pastor Oskar Pfister remained friends for decades.
Pfister’s reply “The Illusion of a Future” simply turns Freud’s book title around.

teile.einleitung: Conservative Judaism is a movement in Judaism that stands between Orthodoxy and Reform Judaism. It holds to the religious laws, but understands them as something that has developed in history. Outside North America the movement is called Masorti.
wichtigste: The rabbi Zacharias Frankel is regarded as the founder of the movement.
From 1854 Frankel led the Jewish Theological Seminary in Breslau.
In Israel and Europe the movement is called Masorti, which means “traditional”.
From 1902 Solomon Schechter led the Jewish Theological Seminary in New York.
Halakha is regarded as binding, but may be developed further if well justified.
In 1985 Amy Eilberg was ordained as the first woman rabbi of this movement.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century Jews in Germany argued about how much may change in religious life. The rabbi **Zacharias Frankel** left a rabbis’ assembly in 1845 because it wanted to push back **Hebrew** in worship. He founded the **“positive-historical school”**. His position between Reform and Orthodoxy is seen as the origin of Conservative Judaism.

From **1854** Frankel led the **Jewish Theological Seminary of Breslau**. There future rabbis learned the traditional teaching and at the same time modern **scholarship**. Many well-known scholars came from this school. In 1938 the seminary was closed by the Nazis.

In the USA the movement became particularly large. The scholar **Solomon Schechter** had recovered thousands of old manuscripts from the **Cairo Geniza**. From **1902** he led the **Jewish Theological Seminary** in New York and built it up into the centre of Conservative Judaism. **Mordecai Kaplan** taught there too, and Reconstructionist Judaism arose at his suggestion.

**Halakha** is Jewish religious law. Conservative Judaism holds it to be **binding**. But it allows adjustments if they are well justified, because the law has developed in the past as well. Outside North America, for example in Israel, the movement is called **Masorti**, which means “traditional”.

In **1985** **Amy Eilberg** was ordained at the Jewish Theological Seminary as the first woman rabbi. There had been women rabbis earlier in other movements: **Regina Jonas** in 1935 in Germany and **Sally Priesand** in 1972 in Reform Judaism. Today women in Conservative congregations can take on many religious tasks.

gewusst: In the Cairo Geniza lay old writings that people did not want to throw away because they might contain the name of God.
Kaplan understood Judaism as an evolving civilisation, not only as a religion.

teile.einleitung: The Ramayana is one of the great heroic epics of India. It tells the story of Prince Rama, his wife Sita and the great battle against the demon king Ravana.
wichtigste: The Ramayana is attributed to the sage Valmiki.
It is written in Sanskrit.
Prince Rama comes from the city of Ayodhya.
Rama has to go into exile in the forest for 14 years.
The demon king Ravana, with his ten heads, abducts Rama’s wife Sita.
The monkey god Hanuman helps Rama to find Sita.
At the festival of Dussehra, large figures of Ravana are burned.

abschnitte.text: The **Ramayana** is a long poem in **Sanskrit**, the ancient language of India. It is attributed to the sage **Valmiki**. The epic consists of seven books and many thousands of verses. Throughout South and South-East Asia the story is still told, acted and danced today.

**Rama** is the eldest son of King **Dasharatha** of **Ayodhya** in northern India. He is supposed to become king. But because of a promise made by his father, he has to live in the forest for **14 years**. His wife **Sita** and his brother **Lakshmana** go with him of their own free will.

In the forest the demon king **Ravana** abducts Sita to his kingdom of **Lanka**. This is where the great battle of the epic begins. Ravana is shown with **ten heads**. They stand for his great learning and power.

Rama finds help among a people of monkeys. The monkey god **Hanuman** leaps over the sea to Lanka in one enormous jump and finds Sita. Afterwards the army of monkeys builds a bridge across the sea. In the great battle Rama defeats Ravana and frees Sita.

At the festival of **Dussehra**, many people in northern India celebrate Rama’s victory over Ravana. Huge figures of Ravana are burned with fireworks. The festival of lights, **Diwali**, also recalls the story in northern India: with lamps, Rama is said to have been welcomed in Ayodhya after his return.

gewusst: In Thailand the story is called the Ramakien, and in Indonesia it is performed as shadow play and dance.
Hanuman is so popular in India that there are temples dedicated to him alone.

teile.einleitung: Navaratri is a major festival in Hinduism. The name means “nine nights”. It celebrates above all the goddess Durga and her victory over a dangerous demon.
wichtigste: Navaratri comes from Sanskrit: “nava” means nine, “ratri” means night.
The most important Navaratri usually falls in September or October.
In the myth the goddess Durga defeats the buffalo demon Mahishasura.
Durga usually rides on a lion or a tiger.
The tenth day is called Vijayadashami or Dussehra.
In Gujarat people dance the Garba and the Dandiya.
In West Bengal the great Durga Puja is celebrated.

abschnitte.text: The name **Navaratri** comes from **Sanskrit**: “nava” means nine, “ratri” means night. So the festival lasts nine nights. There are several Navaratris in the year. The most important is **Sharada Navaratri** in **autumn**, usually in September or October. The exact date follows the Hindu lunar calendar.

At the centre is the goddess **Durga**. She is usually shown with many arms and weapons and rides on a **lion** or tiger. According to the myth, the buffalo demon **Mahishasura** threatened the gods. Durga fought him for nine nights. On the tenth day she defeated him. So the festival stands for the **victory of good over evil**.

In the state of **Gujarat** in western India, people dance every night during Navaratri. In the **Garba**, many people move in a circle, often around a lamp or a picture of the goddess. In the **Dandiya**, the dancers hold colourful **wooden sticks** and strike them against each other in time. Many wear colourful festive clothes. The dances often last until late at night.

In **West Bengal**, **Durga Puja** is celebrated at the same time. In the city of **Kolkata**, elaborate festival pavilions with large figures of Durga are built. At the end the figures are often immersed in a river. The day after the nine nights is called **Vijayadashami** or **Dussehra**. In northern India, large figures of the demon king Ravana are burned on this day.

gewusst: Durga Puja in Kolkata has been on UNESCO’s list of intangible cultural heritage since 2021.
In Switzerland too, Hindu communities celebrate Navaratri in their temples.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Rome, some rulers were worshipped like gods. This worship is called the imperial cult. It was religion and politics at once, and it was meant to hold the huge empire together.
wichtigste: After his death, **Gaius Julius Caesar** was officially raised to the status of a state god, the first Roman to be so.
A deified ruler was called **Divus**.
The **Senate** decided on deification.
In the East, Augustus was worshipped together with the goddess **Roma**.
In 249/250 Emperor **Decius** demanded a sacrifice to the gods from all inhabitants.
Many Christians refused this sacrifice.

abschnitte.text: After Caesar’s murder in 44 BC, a **comet** appeared in the sky. Many Romans saw this as a sign that Caesar had been taken up among the gods. In 42 BC the Senate officially declared him **Divus Julius**. His adopted son **Octavian**, the later Augustus, then called himself **Divi filius**, “son of the deified”. He used this descent for political ends.

When an emperor died, the Senate could declare him a god by a decree. This elevation was called **consecratio**. The emperor then received temples, priests and sacrifices. Emperors whom the Senate rejected were not deified, and some were even condemned and erased from memory. According to the writer **Suetonius**, Emperor **Vespasian** joked on his deathbed: “Alas, I think I am becoming a god.”

In the eastern part of the empire it was usual to worship rulers even in their lifetime. There Augustus allowed temples only together with the goddess **Roma**, for example in **Pergamon**. In this way Rome itself and the ruler were honoured. In **Lugdunum**, today’s Lyon, the altar of the three Gauls for Roma and Augustus was dedicated around 12/10 BC. Every year representatives of the Gallic tribes gathered there. In this way the imperial cult strengthened the bond between the provinces and Rome.

For Jews and Christians there was only one God, so they refused to sacrifice to the emperor as a god. In the year 249/250, Emperor **Decius** demanded a sacrifice to the gods from all inhabitants of the empire. Anyone who had sacrificed received a written certificate, a so-called **libellus**. Many Christians refused the sacrifice and were persecuted for it. Only in the 4th century was Christianity permitted and promoted in the empire.

gewusst: Some of these certificates of sacrifice from the time of Decius have survived on papyrus in Egypt.
The month of July is named after Gaius Julius Caesar, and August after Augustus.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, people with many different religions live side by side, and more and more people belong to no religion. The Federal Statistical Office regularly counts how the population is made up.
wichtigste: In 2023 around 36 per cent of the population aged 15 and over were **non-denominational**.
Around 31 per cent in 2023 were Roman Catholic, and around 19 per cent Evangelical Reformed.
At around 6 per cent, **Islam** is the largest non-Christian religion.
The figures are collected by the **Federal Statistical Office** (FSO).
The first federal census took place in 1850.
Since 2010, annual sample surveys have replaced the large census.

abschnitte.text: Since the **Reformation** in the 16th century, cantons were shaped as either Catholic or Reformed. This division led to quarrels and even wars and shaped Swiss history into the 20th century. In the 19th century the Reformed denomination was still the majority. Around 1970 almost half the population belonged to the Reformed Church.

abschnitte.titel: More and more people with no denomination
abschnitte.text: A person is **non-denominational** if they belong to no religious community. Their share has grown strongly in recent decades. Already in 2022 the non-denominational were ahead of the Roman Catholics, and in 2023 they were around 36 per cent. The share of Reformed fell from around 21 per cent in 2022 to around 19 per cent in 2023. According to the FSO, men are more often non-denominational than women.

Around 6 per cent of the population belong to an **Islamic community**. Many Muslims have roots in the Balkans or in Turkey. In addition there are Orthodox Christians, free churches, Jews, Hindus and Buddhists. Many of these communities have grown through immigration.

The first **federal census** took place in 1850, shortly after the founding of the federal state. Since then religious affiliation has also been recorded. Until 2000 all residents were surveyed every ten years. Since 2010 the FSO has used registers and annual sample surveys such as the **structural survey**, in which around 200,000 people aged 15 and over provide information.

gewusst: Because only a sample is surveyed, the shares are estimates, which the FSO calculates very precisely.
In Switzerland, religious affiliation has been recorded statistically for over 170 years.

teile.einleitung: Sephardim is the name given to the Jews whose ancestors lived on the Iberian Peninsula, that is, in Spain and Portugal. After their expulsion at the end of the 15th century they spread around the Mediterranean and beyond.
wichtigste: The name comes from the Hebrew word “Sefarad” for the Iberian Peninsula.
In 1492 the Jews had to leave Spain, and a few years later Portugal too.
Many of the expelled found refuge in the Ottoman Empire.
Many Sephardim spoke Ladino, also called Judaeo-Spanish.
Jews who were forcibly baptised but secretly kept their faith were called Marranos.

abschnitte.text: **Sefarad** is a place name from the Bible. In the Middle Ages Jews applied it to Spain and Portugal. The descendants of the Jews from there are therefore called **Sephardim**. Jews from Central and Eastern Europe, by contrast, are called **Ashkenazim**. Both groups have in part their own customs, melodies and pronunciations.

In the year **1492** the Spanish monarchs ordered that all Jews must be baptised or leave the country. Shortly afterwards something similar happened in Portugal. Many Jews were baptised under pressure but secretly went on living according to Jewish tradition. They were called **Marranos**. The **Inquisition**, a church court, persecuted them harshly.

abschnitte.titel: A new home in the Ottoman Empire
abschnitte.text: Sultan **Bayezid II** allowed many refugees to settle in the **Ottoman Empire**. They lived in places such as Istanbul, Izmir and **Thessaloniki**. In Thessaloniki Jews then made up the majority of the population for centuries. Other Sephardim moved to North Africa, Italy or later to **Amsterdam**. A famous Portuguese synagogue stands there to this day.

Many Sephardim spoke **Ladino**, also called Judaeo-Spanish. It is based on Old Spanish and took in words from Hebrew, Turkish and other languages. For a long time Ladino was written in Hebrew letters. Today only a few people speak it, but songs and stories are kept alive.

gewusst: In Thessaloniki, Jews were the largest population group in the city for centuries.
Ladino is a language on a Spanish basis that was long written in Hebrew script.

teile.einleitung: Pax is the Latin word for peace. You find it on churches, on flags and in the history of ancient Rome.
wichtigste: Pax means peace.
Latin was the language of the ancient Romans and for a long time the language of the Church.
For the Romans, Pax was also a goddess of peace.
The “Pax Romana” was a long period of peace in the Roman Empire.
Peace flags often bear the Italian word “Pace”.

abschnitte.text: **Pax** is Latin and means **peace**. Latin was the language of the ancient Romans. Later it long remained the language of the Catholic Church. That is why you often read the word on churches or on gravestones, for example in “Requiescat in pace”, which means “May he rest in peace”.

For the Romans, **Pax** was also a goddess who embodied peace. Emperor Augustus had a great altar of peace built in Rome, the **Ara Pacis**. The long period with few wars in the Roman Empire is called the **Pax Romana**, the Roman peace.

In the Christian service, people wish each other peace. The priest says: “Peace be with you.” Afterwards many shake hands. In Latin this greeting is “Pax vobiscum”. The **dove** with an olive branch is also a well-known sign of peace.

gewusst: Many words come from Pax, for example the English “peace” and the French “paix”.
The colourful rainbow flag with the word “Pace” on it is a well-known symbol of the peace movement.

teile.einleitung: A name day is the feast day of a saint who has the same first name as you. It is celebrated above all in Catholic and Orthodox regions. Some people even like celebrating it as much as their birthday.
wichtigste: A name day is the feast day of a saint with the same name.
In the calendar, every day belongs to one or more saints.
The custom is common above all among Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
The day often commemorates the saint’s day of death.
Many names have several possible name days, because there are several saints.

abschnitte.text: The Church has a **calendar of saints**. In it, every day of the year belongs to one or more **saints**. Often it is the day on which the saint died. Anyone with the same **first name** celebrates their **name day** on this day. For example, someone called Niklaus often celebrates on 6 December, the day of Saint Nicholas.

In the past Catholic parents often gave their children the name of a saint. The saint was then regarded as their **patron saint**, that is, a special protector. In many families the name day was more important than the birthday. After the **Reformation**, name days were celebrated less often in Reformed areas. In Catholic regions the custom stayed alive.

Today many people celebrate their name day with a small greeting, a cake or a present. In **Poland**, **Greece** and other countries the name day is still very popular. In Catholic parts of **Switzerland** too, people sometimes congratulate one another. Many calendars and diaries show the matching names for each day.

gewusst: Because there are several saints with the same name, some first names have several name days in the year.
Brother Klaus, the patron saint of Switzerland, has his feast day in Switzerland on 25 September.

teile.einleitung: In many religions, people also show their faith through clothing. Some garments are worn only by clergy, others by believers in everyday life. Often you can tell from someone’s clothes which religion they belong to.
wichtigste: A Catholic bishop wears the **mitre** at solemn services.
The Pope mostly wears white.
Reformed ministers often wear a black **gown**.
Sikh men wear a **turban**.
Some Muslim women wear a **headscarf**.
Jewish men wear the prayer shawl, the **tallit**, at morning prayer.

abschnitte.text: The **mitre** is the tall, pointed hat of a Catholic bishop, with one point at the front and one at the back. In everyday life the **Pope** wears a white robe and a small white cap. In many Reformed churches in Switzerland, the ministers wear a black **gown**, a long robe, during the service. Monks in a monastery wear a plain **habit**, often with a hood. You can tell from its colour which order a monk belongs to.

Many Jewish men wear a **kippah**, a small round cap. At morning prayer they put on the **tallit**, a prayer shawl with fringes at the four corners. The fringes are meant to remind them of God’s commandments. In Judaism, covering the head during prayer is a sign of respect for God.

abschnitte.titel: In Islam and among the Sikhs
abschnitte.text: Many Muslim women wear a **headscarf**, others do not. Whether a woman wears one is a personal and religious decision. Among the **Sikhs**, men do not cut their hair and wear it under a **turban**. The turban is an important sign of their faith.

Buddhist monks and nuns mostly wear simple robes. Depending on the country they are, for example, orange, yellow, brown or dark red. They usually shave their heads very short. This shows that appearance is not important to them and that they want to lead a simple life.

gewusst: Christian men take their hats off in church, whereas in synagogues and among the Sikhs the head is covered.
You can recognise the Pope anywhere in the world by his white robe.

teile.einleitung: Obon is a major festival in Japan at which people honour the souls of their ancestors. According to belief, the dead return to their families for a few days. The festival originally comes from Buddhism.
wichtigste: At Obon, people in Japan honour the souls of their ancestors.
It is usually celebrated from 13 to 16 August, but in Tokyo and other places already in July.
The festival goes back to a Buddhist story.
The traditional dance is called Bon Odori.
At Toro Nagashi, paper lanterns are set afloat on the water.
In Kyoto, large fires in the shape of characters burn on 16 August.
Obon is one of Japan’s biggest travel periods.

abschnitte.text: According to belief, at **Obon** the **souls of the dead** return to their families for a few days. They are welcomed with small fires or lanterns in front of the house. At the household altar, food and flowers are set out. Many families visit and clean the **graves** of their ancestors. At the end the souls are sent off again with rituals.

Obon goes back to a **Buddhist** story. A disciple of Buddha wanted to help his dead mother, who was suffering in the afterlife. Buddha advised him to give gifts to the monks. In this way the mother was freed, and the disciple danced for joy. Today the festival combines Buddhist customs with old **ancestor worship**. It is usually celebrated from **13 to 16 August**, but in Tokyo and some other areas already in **July**.

A funny custom: sticks are pushed into a **cucumber** so that it looks like a **horse**. On it the souls are supposed to come home quickly. An **aubergine** is made into a **cow**. On it the souls are supposed to return slowly to the afterlife at the end. In this way the ancestors can be kept with the family for as long as possible.

The dance **Bon Odori** is part of the festival. Many people dance in a circle around a platform on which **drummers** play. They often wear light summer kimonos, called yukata. At the end of Obon, in some places, glowing **paper lanterns** are set on the water. This custom is called **Toro Nagashi**. The lanterns are meant to accompany the souls back to the afterlife.

abschnitte.titel: Fires in Kyoto and crowded trains
abschnitte.text: In **Kyoto**, five large fires burn on mountains around the city on **16 August**. This is called **Gozan no Okuribi**. The best-known fire shows the character for **“great”**. Because at Obon many people travel to their **home towns**, trains and roads are very crowded. Obon is one of the biggest travel periods in Japan.

gewusst: Obon is not an official public holiday in Japan, yet many people have the week off.
The character for “great” in Kyoto is so huge that you can see it from many places in the city.

teile.einleitung: The Sun Dance is one of the most important ceremonies of the Lakota and other peoples of the North American prairie. The dancers pray for several days for the well-being of their community. For a long time the ceremony was banned in the USA.
wichtigste: The Lakota are the westernmost group of the Sioux.
The Sun Dance takes place in summer and usually lasts four days.
In the middle of the dance ground stands a cottonwood tree as a sacred tree.
The dancers fast during the ceremony.
From 1883 the Sun Dance was banned; since 1978 it has been protected by law.

abschnitte.text: The **Lakota** belong to the **Sioux**; they are their westernmost group. In the past they lived as bison hunters on the **Great Plains**, the great prairie of North America. The **bison** was most important to them. It supplied meat, hides, tools and material for the tents. It was regarded as a gift and was treated with reverence.

According to Lakota tradition, **White Buffalo Calf Woman** brought them the sacred pipe. She also taught them important rituals. The birth of a **white bison calf** is therefore still regarded as a special sign today. Also sacred to the Lakota are the **Black Hills** in South Dakota, which they call Paha Sapa. Today the Mount Rushmore monument stands there, which many Lakota feel as an insult.

The Sun Dance takes place in **early summer** or summer, usually around the time of the longest days. Many families gather for it. First the participants cleanse themselves in the **sweat lodge**, where water is poured over hot stones. A **cottonwood** is ceremonially felled and set up in the middle of the dance ground. The dancers dance around this tree, pray and usually **fast** for four days.

The government of the USA banned the Sun Dance from **1883**. It wanted the indigenous peoples to give up their religion. Many nonetheless carried on the ceremony in secret. Only the American Indian Religious Freedom Act of **1978** explicitly protected such ceremonies. Today the Sun Dance is celebrated openly again, often without outside spectators.

gewusst: The birth of a white bison calf is still regarded as a sacred sign by the Lakota.
For almost a hundred years the Lakota had to celebrate their most important ceremony in secret.

teile.einleitung: Rosh Hashanah is the Jewish New Year festival. It usually falls in September or early October. With it begins a special time of reflection and repentance.
wichtigste: **Rosh Hashanah** means “head of the year”.
The festival falls on 1 Tishri, in our calendar in September or October.
In September 2026 the Jewish year **5787** began.
Rosh Hashanah begins the **ten days of repentance**, which end with Yom Kippur.
People greet each other with “Shana tova”, a good year.
Typical are the sound of the **shofar** and apples with honey.

abschnitte.text: Rosh means “head” and Shana means “year”. The festival falls at the beginning of the month of **Tishri** in the Jewish calendar, which follows the moon. That is why in our calendar it falls on a different date every year, usually in September or early October. According to tradition, the Jewish count of years begins with the creation of the world. In this way the year 5787 began in September 2026.

On Rosh Hashanah, Jews think about the past year. In the synagogue the **shofar** is blown, a ram’s horn meant to call people to repent. With the festival begin the **ten days of repentance**. They end on 10 Tishri with **Yom Kippur**, the Day of Atonement.

People greet each other with “**Shana tova**”, which means “good year”. Often they say it more fully, “Shana tova u-metuka”, a good and sweet year. That is why people eat apples dipped in honey. The **challah**, the festive bread, is baked round on Rosh Hashanah instead of long and plaited. The round shape stands for the cycle of the year.

A special custom is called **Tashlich**. People go to a river, a lake or another body of flowing water. There they throw breadcrumbs into the water. This is a sign of symbolically casting away one’s own mistakes and sins and starting afresh.

gewusst: Rosh Hashanah is usually celebrated for two days, even in Israel.
The word Tashlich means “you will cast”.

teile.einleitung: Osiris was one of the most important gods in ancient Egypt. He ruled over the realm of the dead and stood for the hope that a new life begins after death.
wichtigste: Osiris was the king of the realm of the dead.
His brother Seth killed him out of jealousy.
His wife Isis gathered the parts of his body and brought him back to life with magic.
His son is the falcon-headed god Horus.
Osiris was often painted with green skin, as a sign of new life.
Every pharaoh was regarded as the living Horus and, after death, as Osiris.

abschnitte.text: According to the myth, Osiris was at first a good king on earth. His brother **Seth**, the god of chaos and the desert, was jealous of him. He killed Osiris and cut his body into pieces. He scattered the parts all over Egypt.

The goddess **Isis**, the wife of Osiris, gathered all the parts together. With her magic she brought him back to life. But Osiris did not return to earth, and became **king of the dead** instead. Isis was one of the most important goddesses of Egypt.

The son of Osiris and Isis is **Horus**, a god with a falcon’s head. He avenged his father and fought Seth for a long time for the throne. In the end Horus won. That is why every **pharaoh** was regarded as the living Horus and, after his death, as Osiris.

According to Egyptian belief, the dead came before a court. There their heart was weighed against the feather of **Maat**, the goddess of truth and order. Osiris sat there as ruler on his throne. Anyone who had led a good life was allowed to go on living in the afterlife.

Osiris was usually shown like a **mummy**. In his hands he holds a crook and a flail, the symbols of royal power. His skin is often **green** or black. Green stood for the growing of plants, black for the fertile soil along the Nile.

gewusst: The Egyptians shaped small figures of Osiris from earth and grains of corn. When the grains sprouted, it showed the return of life.
An important place of worship of Osiris was the city of Abydos in Upper Egypt.

teile.einleitung: “Sat Sri Akal” is a greeting used by many Sikhs. It means roughly “God is truth”. With it, believers remind themselves of their faith even as they greet each other.
wichtigste: **Sat Sri Akal** is a greeting of the **Sikhs**.
It means roughly “God is truth” or “True is the eternal God”.
The greeting comes from the **Punjabi** language.
Sikhism arose in the **Punjab** in the north of India.
The founder of the religion was **Guru Nanak**.

abschnitte.text: Sat means “truth” or “true”, Sri is a word of honour, and **Akal** means “timeless” or “eternal”. Together the greeting means roughly “True is the eternal God”. Many Sikhs press their palms together in front of the chest when greeting. The greeting is used on meeting and also on parting.

**Sikhism** arose in the 15th and 16th centuries in the **Punjab**, a region in the north of India and in Pakistan. Its founder was **Guru Nanak**. Nine more gurus followed him. Sikhs believe in a single God. Their holy scripture is called the **Guru Granth Sahib**. Many Sikh men wear a turban.

Sikhs also live in Switzerland. Their house of worship is called a **gurdwara**. In **Langenthal** in the canton of Bern there is a large Sikh temple. In every gurdwara there is a communal kitchen, the **langar**. There all visitors receive a free meal, whatever their religion.

gewusst: Besides “Sat Sri Akal”, Sikhs also know a longer greeting: “Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh”.

teile.einleitung: The Mahabharata is a huge heroic poem from ancient India. It is one of the longest epics in the world and a very important text for Hindus. It tells of the quarrel of two related families, which ends in a great battle.
wichtigste: The sage Vyasa is regarded as its author.
According to the legend, the god Ganesha wrote the epic down.
It is one of the longest epics in the world.
The five Pandava brothers fight against their cousins, the Kauravas.
The great battle takes place on the field of Kurukshetra and lasts 18 days.
Krishna advises the archer Arjuna.

abschnitte.text: The Mahabharata is ascribed to the sage **Vyasa**. According to the legend, he even appears in the story himself. A well-known tale says: Vyasa recited the epic, and the elephant-headed god **Ganesha** wrote everything down without a pause. The Mahabharata is composed in the ancient Indian language **Sanskrit**.
